 Summary
 A controlled human infection study published in Science Translational Medicine shows that pre-existing dengue immunity, not the virus alone, determines how much dengue replicates in a person and how durable the resulting protection is — and that the strongest protection comes from moderate, not maximal, viral replication. Leah Katzelnik is senior author on the paper, discussed here by host Vincent Racaniello of Columbia with Brienne Barker of Drew University, Kathy Spindler of the University of Michigan, and Alan Dove.
 Most of the 109 minutes goes to two virology papers: the dengue challenge study (roughly 40 minutes) and a Cell Reports paper from Andrew Mehle's lab on how influenza nucleoprotein blocks the immune sensor RIG-I from detecting the cell's own small RNAs. The rest is news (doctors elected in the 2026 US midterms, 485 locally acquired dengue cases in Florida), listener email, and picks. The title's "challenging dengue" is fair; "RIGging flu" covers the second paper only.
 The dengue work matters beyond dengue because it maps, in humans, which immune measurements predict protection versus enhancement — the correlates any dengue vaccine must hit. The influenza paper describes a countermeasure that may be shared across negative-strand RNA viruses.
 Moderate viremia produces the most durable immunity; high viremia produces the weakest
 The study's central finding inverts intuition: among people with prior dengue immunity, those with the highest viremia mounted the weakest long-term antibody and T-cell responses, while those with intermediate viremia mounted the most potent and enduring ones. The authors write that rapid activation of effector functions "can come at the expense of generating a high-quality, lasting, adaptive immunity."
 The mechanism they propose runs through IL-12. High viremia drove elevated IL-12/IL-23 at day 9, which pushed B cells toward short-lived plasmablast differentiation rather than high-affinity long-lived plasma cells — a pathway previously described in Salmonella infection. The high-viremia group showed greater plasmablast expansion and faster decay of neutralizing antibodies. It also showed a rapid decline in interferon-gamma-positive activated T cells by days 28 and 90, which the authors attribute to a delayed type 1 interferon response impairing survival of activated T cells. The intermediate group peaked at day 28 instead — slower but more durable.
 Viremia group n Dominant prior immunity Antibody/T-cell outcome 
 Low (near zero) 8 Mostly polytypic (multiple prior infections) Potent neutralizing antibodies against conserved quaternary epitopes; minimal replication 
 Intermediate 12 Mostly heterotypic Greatest expansion of dengue-specific CD8 cells; most persistent neutralizing antibodies 
 High 11 Mostly heterotypic Highest plasmablast expansion, fastest antibody decay, T-cell collapse by day 28–90 
 Barker's framing: vaccine developers should not optimize for replication level or raw antibody titer, because the best long-term memory requires balance across several response types.
 Antibody-dependent enhancement is the master variable, and a cell-culture assay predicts it
 Dengue's four serotypes make repeat infection dangerous: antibodies from a first infection bind a second serotype without neutralizing it, ushering the virus into Fc-receptor-bearing myeloid cells it cannot otherwise infect. The result is higher viremia and, in severe cases, plasma leak, shock, hemorrhage, and death. Racaniello notes this dynamic destroyed multiple prior dengue vaccine programs.
 In the trial, the single strongest linear predictor of viremia was fold enhancement of dengue-3 infection by participant serum at a 1:10 dilution, measured in cells engineered to express all three Fc receptors. Neutralizing antibody titers to dengue 3 predicted protection instead. Participants with heterotypic or low-polytypic immunity had more enhancing antibody, less mature neutralizing antibody, and higher viral loads.
 Dove's point: because the human challenge results line up with the Fc-receptor cell-culture readout, vaccine developers gain a cheap assay for enhancement risk before running human studies.
 The paper also reports that even mild enhancement hampers intracellular antiviral responses and produces delayed, sustained inflammation. The authors suggest early therapeutic immunomodulation, possibly with antivirals, to limit replication and improve long-term immunity, and say such drugs will soon be evaluated in Phase 3 trials to prevent progression to severe dengue. Barker cautions that immunomodulation must not suppress the responses needed for durable memory.
 Broadly protective antibodies require sequential exposure — a constraint on vaccine design
 Only people with more than one prior dengue infection carried antibodies against the envelope dimer epitope (EDE), a quaternary site spanning two envelope proteins that is conserved across serotypes and broadly neutralizing. People with potent EDE antibodies showed minimal replication after challenge. The practical implication, per Racaniello: a dengue vaccine must induce responses to all four serotypes, because sequential exposure is what generates the broadly active antibodies.
 Antibodies to NS1 across multiple serotypes also helped. Participants with NS1 binding breadth, typically people who had lived in a dengue-endemic area, partially controlled replication. The authors argue vaccines that induce humoral and possibly cellular immunity to non-structural proteins like NS1 may not reduce viremia but could prevent severe disease and preserve the adaptive response that severe dengue suppresses.
 The trial itself: 45 healthy adults at the NIH in Bethesda received 10^3 ± 10^0.5 PFU of an attenuated dengue-3 vaccine candidate (rDEN3-Δ30-31-7164, carrying a 30-base deletion in the 3' non-coding region) by subcutaneous injection in the deltoid. Samples were collected at days 0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 28, 57, 90, 180, and 365. Three naive participants received a lower dose. One participant developed a Staphylococcus aureus foot infection at day 328, unrelated to the challenge. The authors call the construct "full-length" because, unlike Sanofi's Dengvaxia — chimeric yellow fever backbone carrying only dengue structural proteins — all dengue proteins are present; Racaniello objected that the paper never explains this for non-specialists.
 The "challenge study" label overstates the risk, and the hosts say so
 Barker and Dove both reacted to the phrase "dengue challenge study" with alarm before realizing every participant received an attenuated vaccine strain, not wild-type virus. Barker called it "click-bait-y." Dove: "you challenged with a vaccine — no, that's a vaccine trial." The hosts note the paper references 11 prior dengue challenge studies, all using attenuated viruses, since wild-type dengue cannot ethically be given to volunteers.
 The term is defensible, Dove concedes, because giving even an attenuated strain to someone with prior dengue carries real risk of enhancement — the trial's primary safety question. Spindler notes the title's "controlled human" wording partly mitigates the framing.
 Influenza NP blocks RIG-I from sensing the cell's own phosphorylated small RNAs
 The Cell Reports paper, from first authors Mitchell Ledwith and Thomas Nipper with senior author Andrew Mehle (University of Wisconsin–Madison, with Institut Pasteur and Dalhousie University), describes a countermeasure that works against host self-RNAs rather than viral RNA. Mehle previously appeared on TWiV and is known on the show for the line "science will break your heart."
 RIG-I surveils the cytoplasm for double-stranded RNA bearing a 5' di- or triphosphate. Because cellular RNA vastly outnumbers RIG-I molecules, the sensor cycles rapidly on and off non-immunogenic RNAs and commits only when it finds the phosphate mark. Using a quantitative crosslinking-immunoprecipitation-sequencing method, the authors found that even in infected cells most RIG-I-bound RNAs are host-derived — mainly small non-coding RNAs made by RNA polymerase III, including Y RNAs, VTRNAs, U6, Alu, and tRNAs. Infection increases the fraction of these small RNAs that retain a 5' triphosphate, making them immunogenic and amplifying the interferon response.
 Influenza nucleoprotein (NP) binds these same RNAs. NP and RIG-I co-immunoprecipitate, and the interaction requires RNA. NP binds host non-coding RNAs as well as viral genome — about 25% of NP-bound reads in infected cells are host-derived, and roughly 30% are influenza-derived during infection versus 20% when NP is pre-expressed. Comparing NP expressed alone with NP in infected cells, 1,400 RNAs were differentially bound, showing that infection reshapes NP's RNA partners — something other viral factors contribute to, which the paper does not identify.
 Functionally, RNAs pulled down with NP from infected cells activate an interferon promoter reporter; the same RNAs from uninfected cells do not. Treating the RNA with RNase or removing the 5' triphosphate abolishes activation. A cytoplasm-restricted NP construct completely blocks sensing of triphosphate double-stranded RNA in reporter cells. The authors replicate the findings in primary human bronchial epithelial cells grown at air-liquid interface, though not in animals.
 Dove's analogy: the Pol III transcripts act like a transistor's bias voltage, setting RIG-I's sensitivity so a viral signal pushes it over threshold. Spindler frames it as the system training on itself. The authors note that all negative-strand RNA viruses carry an NP or N protein, and some positive-strand viruses (coronaviruses, nidoviruses) bind RNA without sequence specificity, suggesting a shared strategy worth testing.
 Florida's 485 locally acquired dengue cases signal a widening mosquito range
 CIDRAP reported 485 autochthonous dengue cases in Florida in 2026, up from 62 the prior year. Racaniello attributes the rise to Aedes aegypti range expansion and a sufficient base of infected people to sustain transmission, and expects spread further north. Barker noted there were zero autochthonous cases when she began teaching at Drew. Dove stressed this is not a vaccine-uptake failure: no highly efficacious dengue vaccine exists.
 Separately, CIDRAP reported that six doctors and public health professionals won seats in the 2026 US midterms with support from the 314 Action Fund. Winners named on the show include Amy Acton (governor of Ohio), Abdul El-Sayed (senator from Michigan), pediatrician Ann Andrews (South Carolina Senate), Richard Pan (California), nurse Mitchell Berman (Wisconsin), nurse practitioner Christina Knickerbocker (Ohio), surgeon Adam Hamawy (New Jersey 12th District), and Jasmine Clark, who holds a PhD in microbiology (Georgia House). Dove cautioned that physicians in Congress are a mixed bag, citing a Louisiana physician and a Kentucky senator he did not name favorably.
 Listener mail: RSV vaccination, a student's election reaction, and measles in Fiji
 Lisa, a pro-vaccine mother in Florida, asked why nobody in her Facebook moms group — including her — mentions the RSV vaccine when mothers describe infants hospitalized with RSV. The hosts' consensus: raising vaccination mid-crisis is poorly timed, but a follow-up note that a vaccine exists for children from six months of age could prevent the next hospitalization. Racaniello added that natural RSV infection does not confer good immunity, so vaccination remains worthwhile after recovery. Lisa's own explanation for her silence was fear of backlash.
 Toby, a third-year biomedicine student in Australia sitting his first virology exam, credited TWiV with cementing his interest in virology research. He called Operation Warp Speed the greatest success of the first Trump administration and the greatest public health achievement in his memory, and said he was "dumbfounded" by subsequent US public health decisions. He reported that the day after the US midterms, surging right-wing Australian parties removed all references to Trump from their websites.
 Anthony sent a link to David Morens' article on measles in Fiji in 1875, which recorded roughly 50,000 deaths in a population of 150,000 — about a third — after the islands were annexed to the British Empire. Dove noted Jack London's South Sea Tales contains accounts of measles deliberately introduced to island populations.
 Wes, a press officer for PETA, corrected the hosts' description of the group's tactics, saying PETA sticks to splashing paint on its own members at protests. Mary, a former dairy farmer in Washington and Oregon, explained heifer leasing: heifer operations buy female calves at birth, raise and artificially inseminate them, and a leasing company buys the bred heifers and leases them to milk producers, replacing cows after roughly three years of production. The chain creates many farm-to-farm animal movements that could move influenza virus; she did not know whether heifers are now tested for bird flu.
 Picks and a recurring editorial argument about anthropomorphism
 Spindler's pick is Ben Tonelli's Bird of the Week email, a sub-minute weekly note with four or five facts per bird; her sample covered the mountain chickadee, which caches conifer seeds, dominates lower-ranked birds at high altitude, and lives in groups of four to six adults, with pair bonds that occasionally end in "divorce" when an attractive newcomer joins. Dove's pick is The Dark Frontier by marine biologist Jeffrey Marlow, covering deep-sea hydrothermal systems explored via the Alvin submersible and the emerging push to strip-mine the deep ocean. Barker's pick is coverage of "grandma hobbies" — repetitive handwork such as crocheting — linked to reduced burnout and stronger neural pathways; she connected it to a stressed student who asked to aliquot samples for the calming effect of repetitive pipetting. Racaniello's pick is a Carter Studios Physics video on where photons go when a light is switched off: photons strike walls, excite atoms that re-emit infrared, and escape to space; photons generated in the Sun's core take over 100,000 years to reach the surface and about nine minutes to reach Earth.
 The episode's longest running argument is editorial. Racaniello objects to language that gives viruses agency — "influenza virus antagonizes self-sensing by RIG-I to enhance viral replication" — and to the paper's use of "as" where "because" is meant. Spindler proposed rewording to "suppressing viral replication." Barker said she opens every class with a disclaimer that she anthropomorphizes as shorthand for selection acting on a virus population. Dove pushed back, half-seriously, that the phrasing may be defensible. Racaniello said his textbook with Jane Flint removes such constructions entirely.
 What to watch
 Three threads carry forward. First, the Phase 3 trials of immunomodulators to prevent severe dengue, which the paper says are imminent — their design will test whether the IL-12/plasmablast pathway is a viable target or whether blunting it costs durable immunity. Second, whether the Fc-receptor enhancement assay becomes a standard gate for dengue vaccine candidates, given that it predicted human viremia from a cell-culture readout. Third, whether NP's blockade of host self-RNA sensing generalizes: the authors flag every negative-strand RNA virus as a candidate, which would make this a broad antiviral-target class rather than an influenza curiosity. On the public health side, Florida's case count — 62 to 485 in one year — is the number to track for US vector-borne disease exposure.
 Business Highlights
 Immunomodulatory drugs for dengue must be designed to preserve the immune responses needed for durable memory while dampening the inflammatory cascade, so developers need this kind of detailed immune profiling before late-stage trials.
 Vaccines that induce humoral and cellular immunity to non-structural proteins like NS1 may not reduce viremia but could still prevent severe disease, suggesting a different efficacy endpoint than viral load for dengue vaccine development.
 The study validates a set of assays that can screen vaccine candidates for correlates of protection more cheaply than human challenge studies, which would then be reserved for safety testing. This lowers the cost and risk of dengue vaccine development.
 Findings support combining immunomodulators with antivirals early in enhanced dengue disease, with such drugs reportedly headed to phase 3 trials for preventing progression to severe dengue.
 Key Quotes
 As you're developing that vaccine, you shouldn't necessarily optimize replication level or antibody level, because you need to have this balance between a few different types of responses to get the best long-term memory response.
 Brienne Barker A counterintuitive vaccine-design principle drawn from the dengue challenge data: more replication is not better. This paper also validates a set of tools for assaying your vaccine candidates in easier ways than doing the challenge studies, which you would presumably then do to test safety of the vaccine.
 Alan Dove Frames the study's practical value as a screening toolkit for correlates of protection before costly human challenge work. Counter to existing hypotheses, we found that the rapid activation of the adaptive effector functions come at the expense of developing high-quality enduring adaptive immunity.
 Vincent Racaniello Highlights the paper's headline reversal of the assumption that faster, stronger immune activation is always better. Antibody-dependent enhancement inhibits intracellular antiviral responses and produces a barren immune signaling, enabling the virus to replicate more without triggering a normal, innate, and adaptive response.
 Vincent Racaniello Concise mechanistic explanation of why ADE makes dengue worse rather than better. Any amount of antibody-dependent enhancement, even mild, hampers the antiviral responses. And that's associated with delayed and sustained inflammation that can get worse and worse.
 Vincent Racaniello Argues even subclinical enhancement matters, motivating early immunomodulator plus antiviral treatment. Topics

The authors replicate the findings in primary human bronchial epithelial cells grown at air-liquid interface, though not in animals.
 Dove's analogy: the Pol III transcripts act like a transistor's bias voltage, setting RIG-I's sensitivity so a viral signal pushes it over threshold. Spindler frames it as the system training on itself. The authors note that all negative-strand RNA viruses carry an NP or N protein, and some positive-strand viruses (coronaviruses, nidoviruses) bind RNA without sequence specificity, suggesting a shared strategy worth testing.
 Florida's 485 locally acquired dengue cases signal a widening mosquito range
 CIDRAP reported 485 autochthonous dengue cases in Florida in 2026, up from 62 the prior year. Racaniello attributes the rise to Aedes aegypti range expansion and a sufficient base of infected people to sustain transmission, and expects spread further north. Barker noted there were zero autochthonous cases when she began teaching at Drew. Dove stressed this is not a vaccine-uptake failure: no highly efficacious dengue vaccine exists.
 Separately, CIDRAP reported that six doctors and public health professionals won seats in the 2026 US midterms with support from the 314 Action Fund. Winners named on the show include Amy Acton (governor of Ohio), Abdul El-Sayed (senator from Michigan), pediatrician Ann Andrews (South Carolina Senate), Richard Pan (California), nurse Mitchell Berman (Wisconsin), nurse practitioner Christina Knickerbocker (Ohio), surgeon Adam Hamawy (New Jersey 12th District), and Jasmine Clark, who holds a PhD in microbiology (Georgia House). Dove cautioned that physicians in Congress are a mixed bag, citing a Louisiana physician and a Kentucky senator he did not name favorably.
 Listener mail: RSV vaccination, a student's election reaction, and measles in Fiji
 Lisa, a pro-vaccine mother in Florida, asked why nobody in her Facebook moms group — including her — mentions the RSV vaccine when mothers describe infants hospitalized with RSV. The hosts' consensus: raising vaccination mid-crisis is poorly timed, but a follow-up note that a vaccine exists for children from six months of age could prevent the next hospitalization. Racaniello added that natural RSV infection does not confer good immunity, so vaccination remains worthwhile after recovery. Lisa's own explanation for her silence was fear of backlash.
 Toby, a third-year biomedicine student in Australia sitting his first virology exam, credited TWiV with cementing his interest in virology research. He called Operation Warp Speed the greatest success of the first Trump administration and the greatest public health achievement in his memory, and said he was "dumbfounded" by subsequent US public health decisions. He reported that the day after the US midterms, surging right-wing Australian parties removed all references to Trump from their websites.
 Anthony sent a link to David Morens' article on measles in Fiji in 1875, which recorded roughly 50,000 deaths in a population of 150,000 — about a third — after the islands were annexed to the British Empire. Dove noted Jack London's South Sea Tales contains accounts of measles deliberately introduced to island populations.
 Wes, a press officer for PETA, corrected the hosts' description of the group's tactics, saying PETA sticks to splashing paint on its own members at protests. Mary, a former dairy farmer in Washington and Oregon, explained heifer leasing: heifer operations buy female calves at birth, raise and artificially inseminate them, and a leasing company buys the bred heifers and leases them to milk producers, replacing cows after roughly three years of production. The chain creates many farm-to-farm animal movements that could move influenza virus; she did not know whether heifers are now tested for bird flu.
 Picks and a recurring editorial argument about anthropomorphism
 Spindler's pick is Ben Tonelli's Bird of the Week email, a sub-minute weekly note with four or five facts per bird; her sample covered the mountain chickadee, which caches conifer seeds, dominates lower-ranked birds at high altitude, and lives in groups of four to six adults, with pair bonds that occasionally end in "divorce" when an attractive newcomer joins. Dove's pick is The Dark Frontier by marine biologist Jeffrey Marlow, covering deep-sea hydrothermal systems explored via the Alvin submersible and the emerging push to strip-mine the deep ocean. Barker's pick is coverage of "grandma hobbies" — repetitive handwork such as crocheting — linked to reduced burnout and stronger neural pathways; she connected it to a stressed student who asked to aliquot samples for the calming effect of repetitive pipetting. Racaniello's pick is a Carter Studios Physics video on where photons go when a light is switched off: photons strike walls, excite atoms that re-emit infrared, and escape to space; photons generated in the Sun's core take over 100,000 years to reach the surface and about nine minutes to reach Earth.
 The episode's longest running argument is editorial. Racaniello objects to language that gives viruses agency — "influenza virus antagonizes self-sensing by RIG-I to enhance viral replication" — and to the paper's use of "as" where "because" is meant. Spindler proposed rewording to "suppressing viral replication." Barker said she opens every class with a disclaimer that she anthropomorphizes as shorthand for selection acting on a virus population. Dove pushed back, half-seriously, that the phrasing may be defensible. Racaniello said his textbook with Jane Flint removes such constructions entirely.
 What to watch
 Three threads carry forward. First, the Phase 3 trials of immunomodulators to prevent severe dengue, which the paper says are imminent — their design will test whether the IL-12/plasmablast pathway is a viable target or whether blunting it costs durable immunity. Second, whether the Fc-receptor enhancement assay becomes a standard gate for dengue vaccine candidates, given that it predicted human viremia from a cell-culture readout. Third, whether NP's blockade of host self-RNA sensing generalizes: the authors flag every negative-strand RNA virus as a candidate, which would make this a broad antiviral-target class rather than an influenza curiosity. On the public health side, Florida's case count — 62 to 485 in one year — is the number to track for US vector-borne disease exposure.
 Business Highlights
 Immunomodulatory drugs for dengue must be designed to preserve the immune responses needed for durable memory while dampening the inflammatory cascade, so developers need this kind of detailed immune profiling before late-stage trials.
 Vaccines that induce humoral and cellular immunity to non-structural proteins like NS1 may not reduce viremia but could still prevent severe disease, suggesting a different efficacy endpoint than viral load for dengue vaccine development.
 The study validates a set of assays that can screen vaccine candidates for correlates of protection more cheaply than human challenge studies, which would then be reserved for safety testing. This lowers the cost and risk of dengue vaccine development.
 Findings support combining immunomodulators with antivirals early in enhanced dengue disease, with such drugs reportedly headed to phase 3 trials for preventing progression to severe dengue.
